description.summary: A Caribbean water guardian spirit, particularly prominent in Trinidad and Tobago, depicted as a beautiful woman from the waist up with the lower body of a great snake. She protects rivers, streams, and the animals that live in them.
description.full: Mama Dlo (also Mama D'Leau or Mama Glo) is a folkloric water spirit of the southern Caribbean, especially associated with Trinidad and Tobago, but also with Saint Lucia and Dominica. Her name comes from French Creole 'Maman de l'Eau' — 'Mother of the Water'. She is described as a beautiful woman from the waist up, with long hair that she combs with a golden comb, and a forked tongue; from the waist down her body twists into the coils of a great snake. She functions as a protector and healer of rivers, streams, and the animals that live in them, and is said to punish those who pollute the waters, hunt out of season, or otherwise abuse the natural world. Her tradition draws on West African water-spirit complexes (notably Mami Wata), French Creole and Indigenous Caribbean elements, and she is sometimes paired in oral tradition with the forest guardian Papa Bois.

etymology.origin: French Creole 'Maman de l'Eau' ('Mother of the Water'), reflecting the French-Creole strata of Trinidadian and wider Lesser Antillean folklore.
etymology.meaning: 'Mother of the Water' — a guardian spirit of fresh water, particularly rivers and streams.
etymology.first_use: Recorded in Caribbean folklore collections from the 20th century; oral tradition is older.

related_phenomena.name: Mami Wata
related_phenomena.description: West African water spirit complex from which Caribbean water mothers partly derive

related_phenomena.name: Iara
related_phenomena.description: Brazilian water-spirit woman of Tupi-Guarani tradition

related_phenomena.name: Papa Bois
related_phenomena.description: Trinidadian forest guardian, sometimes paired with Mama Dlo in oral tradition

features.feature: Beautiful upper body of a woman
features.description: Long-haired woman from the waist up
From the waist down her body twists into the coils of a great snake
Carries a golden comb that she draws through her long hair

physical.morphology: Composite serpent-woman: human female torso joined to a large snake's body, often described as anaconda-like.

abilities.description: Protects rivers, streams, and pools, and the creatures that live in them
Said to lure, drown, or otherwise punish those who poison fish, dynamite rivers, hunt wantonly, or pollute waters
Cares for and heals the animals of the rivers she presides over

patterns: Encountered at remote river bends and pools
Often seen combing her hair on a rock
Aggressive toward those who harm rivers or wildlife; benign or helpful to those who show respect

range.description: Folkloric tradition of the southern Caribbean, particularly Trinidad and Tobago, with related figures in Saint Lucia and Dominica.

hotspots.name: Trinidad rivers and forests

location.description: Inland rivers, streams, and forested waterways of Trinidad

hotspots.notes: Heart of the Mama Dlo tradition; figure cited in environmental and folkloric education.

first_recorded.source: Caribbean folklore collections; oral tradition older

peak_activity_periods.description: Mama Dlo features prominently in published Trinidadian folklore collections, school curricula, and environmental storytelling.

origins.cultural_roots: Trinidadian Creole folklore drawing on West African water-spirit traditions (notably Mami Wata), French and French-Creole storytelling, and Indigenous Caribbean elements.
origins.earliest_accounts: Oral tradition; entered the published record through 20th-century collections of Trinidadian folklore.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of a broad New World water-mother complex that includes Mami Wata (West Africa), Iara (Brazil), and Madre de Aguas (Cuba).

timeline.event: Mama Dlo enters the published folklore record through Trinidadian and wider Caribbean folklore collections
timeline.significance: Establishes her as a named Caribbean folk figure

history.modern_era: Mama Dlo is widely cited in Trinidadian environmental education and children's literature as a guardian of rivers and forests, and remains an active figure in cultural performance, festival, and ecological storytelling.

paranormal.name: Caribbean water spirit
paranormal.description: Mama Dlo is a genuine guardian spirit of fresh water, descended from West African Mami Wata traditions and adapted in the Caribbean.
evidence_cited: Continuity of oral tradition across generations
Parallels with Mami Wata and other water-mother figures

skeptical.name: Folkloric / didactic figure
skeptical.description: Mama Dlo is a teaching figure of Trinidadian folklore: a personification used to enforce respect for rivers, fish stocks, and forest ecology, rather than a creature of zoological reality.
evidence_cited: Clear didactic structure of the tales
Consistent moralizing framing in collected versions

traditions: Trinidadian Creole folktales of forest and river guardians
French-Creole storytelling traditions of the Lesser Antilles
stories: Tales of fishermen punished for poisoning rivers
Encounters with a beautiful woman combing her hair at a riverside pool
folklore.beliefs: Within Trinidadian folk tradition, Mama Dlo is treated as a real and powerful guardian of fresh water; respect for rivers and the creatures within them is owed to her.

indigenous.significance: Mama Dlo's tradition is rooted in Afro-Caribbean Creole culture; she is not specifically an Indigenous Caribbean figure, though she shares motifs with broader water-mother traditions.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Treat Mama Dlo as a living folk figure of Trinidad and Tobago; do not flatten her into a generic 'mermaid' or detach her from her Afro-Caribbean and French-Creole context.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Caribbean sources where possible; preserve the connection to Mami Wata and to Trinidadian environmental ethics.

literature: Trinidadian folklore collections featuring Mama Dlo / Mama D'Leau
Hans E. A. Boos, The Snakes of Trinidad and Tobago (2001)
other: Often depicted alongside Papa Bois in Trinidadian cultural performance, Carnival mas, and educational material

research.ongoing_studies: Mama Dlo is studied within Caribbean folklore, gender studies, and environmental humanities rather than as a cryptozoological subject.

sources.title: The Snakes of Trinidad and Tobago
